The 40th Personnel Centre is, in practical terms, abolished following Operation Storm and Operation Flash. The members of the SVK who were handled by the 40th Personnel Centre had nowhere to go. They were displaced and arrived as refugees in the FRY. If you put things into that kind of perspective, the chief of General Staff must have had something in mind to the effect that those persons have committed infractions on military discipline and who on earth would try them there unless they were now back home to their place of origin, to gain their livelihood again. But that was after the fall of the Republic of Serbian Krajina and the abolishment of the 40th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand, General, and so do we agree that these actions set out in this order are being taken in respect of possible disciplinary offences which occurred while they were fighting in the SVK?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, again with the following proviso.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Carry on.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These persons asked to gain entry to the chain of command of the VJ. In that case, the General Staff was supposed to take appropriate measures if there was any information indicating that there had been infractions of military discipline. These people had nowhere to go. They asked for appointments to that army. My personal opinion, and that's all it is, an interpretation of this article would be that. I was not myself involved in actually producing this document because I was at the time head of the system and status-related issues administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right, thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Your Honours, there a number of documents which fall into category which require some discussion before I can use them or not use them with General Nikolic. Can I suggest that the general leave the courtroom so that we can discuss those documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, would you please just excuse us. Apparently there's something that the lawyers want to talk about but in your absence. We'll call you once we are ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have a number of documents, not many, but several documents which I would like to use with General Nikolic for the purpose of establishing bias. They fall into three categories. The first two documents relate to proceedings and an indictment issued against General Nikolic in Serbia for favourable treatment of a general in the allocation of housing. The documents concern an indictment and a ruling on appeal brought against the bringing of indictment by General Nikolic. So these are two documents which would establish that he faces charges for abuse of official position which resulted in another general receiving housing to which he was not entitled. Those proceedings have not been determined because General Pavkovic is also a co-accused, and the proceedings have been suspended until the resolution of General Pavkovic's trial here. The second group of documents concerns General Nikolic's membership of an organisation known as the Serbian General and Admiral's Club. The documents concern, first of all, demonstrate his membership of that club. They express -- there is a page that is essentially a motto or a declaration about the importance of officers to an army. There is a work-plan which includes a clause to say that the club shall continue to provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't read it yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: There's a work-plan. There is a code of ethics of which I want -- wish to cite one article, and there are two press releases relating to the decision of this Court in the Haradinaj case, which in the Prosecution's submission may contain statements showing a particular attitude towards the Tribunal and a particular attitude towards the activities or the position the Serb generals find themselves in. The third -- effectively, sir, those documents show, in the Prosecution's submission, a bias against the Tribunal and a bias towards Serb officers who fought in the Bosnian conflict. The final document, sir, is a record of a meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: When you say "a bias towards Serb officers who fought in the Bosnian conflict," you mean a favourable bias in favour of them?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I won't go into the documents because you haven't asked me to, but I can do so if Your Honours require more particular expression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't think you should do so until such time as a ruling is made because otherwise then you are putting them on evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, I understand. The third document, sir, the third category is a single document, it's a record of the collegium, a meeting between members of the General Staff of the VJ and generals of the 30th Personnel Centre in September 2000. The purpose of the meeting was to discuss ongoing training for VRS officers but in the context of that meeting, various -- at which General Nikolic was present, various statements are made regarding or relevant to the harbouring of fugitives by the VRS and by the VJ. And the relevance of that document would be to establish General Nikolic's at least awareness that this was a -- that this activity was occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, with regard to a response as it relates to the first set of documents, could we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Above and beyond the representations that were made in private session as regards to this particular issue, I believe that the threshold has been established for purposes of the issue of impeachment should the Chamber make a determination that such evidence should be pursued. So I'm dealing with the threshold issue because I think that's one of the issues we need to deal with. With regard to the second sets of documents, I think that there's an underlying problem with the manner in which Mr. Thomas has suggested that the impeachment occur in the event that he asks those direct questions from the witness with regard to the witness's bias or lack thereof concerning the Tribunal either for or against, and concerning Serb generals either for or against, and he receives an answer which is contradictory to that which he finds to be contained in these document, then he may well be in a position to use those documents for impeachment purposes. But the issue of that particular issue of bias has not yet been tested. There is an underlying problem here which is in the absence of there being some adoption by the witness concerning the informations contained in these documents, there's an associational travelling problem which we would normally call an associational guilt problem, but it wouldn't be a guilt situation since obviously we are not dealing with the issue of guilt, but rather, it's as if one is a part of an organisation or part of a group each and everything in that group publishes is adopted by all in the group. I suggest to the Chamber that a more appropriate way of dealing with this particular issue, as it relates to the issue of bias, and I have a secondary problem with that, but as it relates to the issue of bias be directly dealt with between question and answer by Mr. Thomas and the witness. He can ask the witness direct questions with regard to the witness's feel about the Tribunal. He can ask direct questions with regard to the witness's feelings about how the Tribunal has treated previous individuals who have appeared before this Tribunal who happen to be Serb generals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a problem with that problem that you have, Mr. Guy-Smith. My problem is that I don't think it is for the Chamber to define or even for the Defence to define the limits within which the Prosecution may ask its questions. We must agree, either the Defence objects to the use of those documents because they don't meet the requirements or if you say they may be used, then --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand your thinking, Your Honour. And with your thinking in mind, the Defence objects to the use of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you must address the question of threshold, how it has not been met.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The issue of threshold has not been met because he has failed to establish that these documents are documents that would, in fact, achieve the purpose for which they are sought to be introduced.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you don't know that until they have been put to the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, this is one of those unfortunate tautological situations that one finds themselves in. It occurs periodically in a trial, and I find myself in one of those now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that argument address the question of requirements of a threshold?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, you know I'm not one to avoid a direct question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't avoid this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I don't intend to, which is why I'm saying you know that I'm not one to avoid a direct question. I believe that the manner in which Mr. Thomas has made the presentation, he does meet the threshold. Although, I have difficulties, I have difficulties, as I've articulated, with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those are the difficulties outside the threshold.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Understood. Understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you have any comments on the fact category?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm getting to the third category right now. If I could have a moment again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The third set -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The third set of documents poses a somewhat of a slightly different legal analysis than that which is contained in the first two, because part of the legal analysis falls into some of the matters that are actually charged within the indictment itself. I notice we are very close to the break. If we could take the break now so I can formulate a short pithy response as regards to the third set, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At page 49 from lines 1 through 7, Mr. Thomas has indicated -- actually it starts at the page before, has indicated the reason why he wishes to use this particular information and he says, and I quote: "And the relevance of that document would be to establish General Nikolic's at least awareness that this was, that this activity was occurring." Looking at the standards that are to be applied here, first of all, even as a threshold matter independent of the issues that are normally discussed with regard to fresh evidence and understanding the Chamber may well be more lenient as it relates to impeachment evidence, the offer made by Mr. Thomas with regard to the issue of why he wishes to use this evidence does not give rise to an issue of impeachment in the first instance. So with regard to the Defence position our first position is that he has failed to make any threshold with regard to the issue of impeachment. He also has failed to, at this point in time by virtue of the fact where we stand in the case, that being it's after the close of the Prosecution's case, he has failed to meet the requirements of 89 -- Rule 89 with regard to this issue being probative on the issue of, and that's what we are referring to here, probative on the issue of credibility. In addition, the document that I believe he wishes to rely upon is XN 59, and I want to make sure that I'm correct in that regard before I go any further, so just a quick nod would be appreciated. Thank you. The document, at least the translation that I have, indicates on the front page that it is unauthorised and not language edited audio recording of discussions. So there is another issue with regard to reliance on this document as it relates to what, assuming for purpose of discussion that there's any probative value whatsoever, as to what was said, who said what, and whether or not we have any basis to be able to deal with its authenticity. Once again a question under Rule 89. And finally, I think that in the manner in which Mr. Thomas suggests he wishes to use the document, that being relevance of the witness's awareness that something was afoot, he fails to take into account and he fails to make the representation, and I doubt he seriously would be questioning the witness with regard to the state of the law at that time, the law that the witness would necessarily have to follow with regard to the general issue. We would object on all of those grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Sir, in my submissions I said that this goes to show at least that General Nikolic was aware that fugitives and potential fugitives, we are talking about more than one, were being harboured. Implicit in that is that any inaction on the part of General Nikolic when faced with this knowledge or when provided with this knowledge is relevant to any reasons that he might have for taking no action. For example, his bias, his sympathies towards those who are being hidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Did he have any duty to take any action?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: He may have as a human being, his country is a party to the genocide convention. His party is a statute to the statute of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The sympathies that he may have, Your Honour, demonstrate a lack of interest in assisting the Tribunal. This was something that was aired freely at a meeting between the highest officers in the VRS and the highest officers of the VJ of which he was a part. And this goes to his -- its relevant to the sensibilities of those who were present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is he not a retired person now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: This was at a time when he was not retired, sir, this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You characterise his duty as more of a civic duty rather than his duty by virtue of his position in the army, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The difficulty, sir, is that we don't know what steps, he took, if any. I need to confront him with the fact that he is aware of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question is I am a step behind you, you are a Step ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question is whether he did have a duty to take any step, because you sound like you characterise his duty as more of a civic duty, and are you saying that by virtue of being a general in the army, he had a duty to act?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, he did, sir, because the army as an organ of the state of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was required to turn over criminals who had been, or alleged criminals indicted by the Tribunal. They are required to comply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, but is that the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, it's anybody who is responsible for complying -- maybe I should put it another way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not my question. Whether he bore that duty to comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The army was hiding people. The bottom line, sir, is that this document shows that the army, the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The VRS was hiding people with the knowledge of the General Staff of the VJ.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The -- and this demonstrates, Your Honours, that everyone is aware of the situation that exists. Everyone is aware that there is a requirement to turn these people over because these people are being hidden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, your argument is going a little further away from the point, in fact. When you are still giving me the impression that it was the VJ which did it, I thought you were closer to it. Now if it is the VRS that does it and the VJ is aware of it, who is not aware of it? We are all aware of it, but what have we done about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Part of the difficulty, sir, is that we are discussing the contents of the document without being allowed to discuss the contents of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, we are discussing your submissions. Your submissions are that at the time he attended this meeting, the VRS was hiding fugitives.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The VJ was aware that the VRS is hiding fugitives, and you are saying that he had a duty. My question is under those circumstances, what duty lay on him?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I should add one more dimension, sir, and that is that the discussion also involves Mladic which means that the -- it's not just the VRS who are hiding. It may be that the document itself is not clear in terms of Mladic, whether we are talking about the VJ hiding him or the VRS hiding him, we are talking about co-operation between the VRS and the VJ with his security detail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I have serious problems with your submissions, Mr. Thomas. You are shifting the goal-posts. It's no longer knowledge, now it's co-operation between the VJ, and it is also no longer the VRS, it could be the VRS and the VJ. I'm not quite sure where your argument is going now.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: That's the difficulty, sir, with not being able to refer to the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may not refer to the document until it is admitted, but you've got to make your argument outside the document, and stay with your argument. Don't shift around.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand. First of all, the General Nikolic is a professional officer in the Yugoslav Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was under an obligation to turn over alleged fugitives, certainly under an obligation to turn over indicted individuals, which Mladic was one. He would have been aware that steps taken by the General Staff of the VJ or the General Staff of the VRS --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, but it is the General Staff of the VJ, or is it the General Staff of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: On Mladic, it's co-operation between the two, it's intelligence share, it's information sharing. That is the reference to Mladic in this document. It is information sharing. In relation to the others, sir, it is the problem of housing being provided for members of the 30th Personnel Centre, and you will recall that General Nikolic was responsible for housing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those first two categories, if I understood Mr. Guy-Smith, he has considered those two. It is the third category, sir, that we are talking about. So the question of housing doesn't seem to come in here. It's the question of being at the least aware of fugitives being hidden away.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: The problem with the fugitives being hidden away is that they needed housing. That was the problem. This is the context in which the discussion takes place in this document, so the VRS are asking the VJ to resolve the housing problem for all of their officers including those who they are hiding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You see again, now there's another shift of the goal-post. Now you are implying that he actively participated in the hiding of the fugitives by providing them with housing.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I don't know if he did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am not sure why do you link housing now, which was in the first category, why do you link it with the third category now?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Because, Your Honour, that's the context in which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was not the context of your first -- if you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I was trying not to disclose the contents of the document, Your Honour. I was trying to be very general about what the essential points of the document are which was that it dealt with the harbouring of fugitives. This was something that he was necessarily --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But, sir, but, sir, even if you were not -- you are trying not to disclose the contents, where you say -- let me quote you. What line was that, Guy-Smith, at page 49?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Page 49. The specific line is line 5 -- and the relevance of that document would be to establish General Nikolic's at least awareness that this was, this was the activity that was occurring.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It starts on line 5 is what I just read to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Right, now, when you made that statement if you then have been able to say that demonstrates that, in fact, he assisted in providing housing for these people, or he assisted in the hiding of the fugitives, not just awareness.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: But I understand Your Honours's point, but the difficulty, sir, is that at the moment I know nothing about what General Nikolic did or did not do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you are going on a fishing expedition.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I want to put to him, sir, that at the very least this was an open topic of discussion in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sure it must be an open topic of discussion everywhere, all over Serbia and all over the world, everybody is aware that these guys are fugitives, that they're being hidden by some people, and that nobody seems to be getting hold of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, in my submission it's relevant that the General Staff knows that they are not being hidden by anybody. They are being hidden by the VRS. They are being hidden by members of the 30th Personnel Centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed. So they may know who is hiding them, what must they do? Go over to the Republika Srpska and grab them from the VRS? I'm not quite sure what your argument is on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: My argument is no more, sir, then it demonstrates a preparedness to go along with not assisting the Tribunal and that that demonstrates a particular bias of this witness. So when Your Honours have to determine whether the witness is being truthful with you on a particular point, you are entitled to take into account the fact that he is pretty ambivalent about whether or not fugitives, for example, are turned over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure, but my problem is that an individual officer in the army, I fail to see how an individual officer in the army has a duty to do something about fugitives who are at large.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, his -- under the Law of the Army, he is required to -- he is required to observe international conventions. He is required to observe International Humanitarian Law. His nation is required as a party to this statute to turn over individuals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: He knows that there is a positive obligation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Of the institution.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, but also as an army officer, if he takes steps or fails to take steps which allow his country to breach its international obligations or result in the army breaching some obligation then that has to be at the very least conduct unbecoming an officer in some respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And what do we expect him to do, if I may just ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: He may have done something, he may have done nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you what would you expect a reasonable officer of the army to do under those circumstances where he doesn't bear the duty within, he is within the structure, but you are saying he is expected to observe International Humanitarian Law. He happens to be aware that another army in the next-door country is harbouring a fugitive, what do you expect him to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: This army is at a meeting with him and others from the General Staff asking for assistance with housing, regulating personnel with training. He could say, look, this is bad for us to be doing this for you when you are harbouring people. We are not going to do it. That's one thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've told you my problem with that argument because that came as an extension later, as a shifting of the goal-posts, so I'm not quite sure, you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour's point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's my problem, it was not part of your original argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Well, I thought it was implicit, sir. He knew at least what I want to ask him is, you know, what he did with this knowledge. I can't say until I put to him what he can say in relation to that. But I can't take the matter any further, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not quite sure whether you have addressed all the other requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can do that, Your Honour. On the question of, I think my learned friend suggested that it needs to be probative on the issue of credibility, my answer to that, sir, is that essentially it's demonstrating a bias either against the Tribunal or in favour of Serb soldiers or Serb officers who may have been considered by this Tribunal to become --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've heard you on that one. I just wanted to -- there are a whole lot of requirements that must be addressed before fresh evidence can be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I'm now talking generally about all three categories, time when you got it, all those.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Yes, sir. I think indicate that the disclosure information I have in relation to the charges and information relating to the housing charges against General Nikolic were disclosed to the Defence on the 2nd of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: This year. As soon as we became aware that General Nikolic was going to be called as a witness, the necessary searches were undertaken, sir. That revealed this information, and that was disclosed on the 2nd of February of this year. The material from the general and admiral's club again was translated as soon as it was obtained in response to General Nikolic being on the list. And this was on the 19th of February with the exception of one document, which was the list of officers of the club, which was disclosed to the Defence on the 26th of February. And the document that we are currently talking about, sir, the minutes of the -- or the record of the meeting between the General Staff and the VRS Main Staff was disclosed on the 11th of February this year. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hate to be leading you, and I don't believe you have exhausted your argument -- the requirements.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I've been passed a note, sir, that the disclosure material was sent on e-court and CD-ROM. It was all on CD-ROM on the dates that I've referred to, sir, and subsequently uploaded into e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Any response, Mr. Guy-Smith?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Only one very brief response. Mr. Thomas said in relationship to this discussion, "I can't say until I put it to him what he can say in relation to that," that's what we classically know as a fishing expedition. That's not impeachment. Submitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas, you may use the first two documents referring to the first two categories and not the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The witness might be brought in. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the Chamber apologises for keeping you outside for so long. Unfortunately it's one of those things that do happen in this kind of work. I hope you don't take it on us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fully understand the need for that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Thank you for understanding.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General, just one other topic that I wanted to deal with you briefly. What is the general and admiral's club of the army of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As in most countries across the world, we in Serbia our decision of the defence minister Davinic established a general and admiral's club. This is a non-party association. It is an association of citizens with no political affiliations whatsoever or indeed any interference in the members officials lives. It is, as I said, a non-party association.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Nikolic. You say it's an association of citizens. Any citizen can become a member, or is it only generals and admirals?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is an association of citizens but in a restricted professional field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: And in this case, we are talking about officers in the army and navy of the VJ; is that right?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The generals and admirals of the VJ and navy too, because that is part of the army. It is a special branch.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. And the work-plan of the club includes that it shall, that is the club, shall continue to provide necessary assistance to individuals on request related to their status, and their obligations with respect to international organisations and institutions, and with respect to the institutions in the country starting out from the state interests of the Republic of Serbia and realistic abilities of the club. Have I understood that section of the work-plan correctly?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the fact that I don't have the statute in front of me, I can hardly be expected to interpret what you are saying. If you can provide a hard copy, I'd be glad to discuss it. For the time being I just don't have it. The statute was adopted by the Assembly as the supreme body of that association.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General, are you a member of the executive board of that club?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Used to be the executive council and now it's the executive board, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Can I ask you if you agree with the following statement: The Hague Tribunal is not a Tribunal but a skillfully packed incrimination of justice that decides who is to be sentenced and how the justice is to be served. Do you agree with that statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. If I agreed with that statement, I certainly wouldn't be sitting here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you agree with the statement that the Tribunal is controlled from within through expert insiders that are used as instruments for keeping the scope of investigations under control?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you agree with the following statement: By acting in this way, the Court got rid of the war criminal and terrorist Ramush Haradinaj due to insufficient evidence because the truth was not supposed to be revealed.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no right to comment on any convictions and sentences before this Tribunal. Therefore, I simply don't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Do you agree with the following statement: The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia did something not a single other country has ever done. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia extradited to the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia the following persons: Its president, the president of the Republic of Serbia, deputy prime minister of the federal government, minister of defence, two chiefs of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, one army commander, and deputy minister of the interior. They were extradited only because they had carried out their duty in a professional manner pursuant to a constitution of a sovereign state. The Federal Republic of Yugoslavia then defended their country from terrorism/separatism and from the NATO aggression. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there were too many sentences in this for me to answer. Can we take it one step at a time? Who said it, whose statement is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: All right. This is a press release that appeared on your website, that is the club of which you are on the executive board, the general and admiral's club of the Republic of Serbia, following the decision in the Haradinaj case. First of all, that answers your first question. That is the source of these statements.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, never was I president of the executive board of the club. Never.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I got no translation. I don't know whether anybody has.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard the interpretation into Serbian of the question posed by Mr. Thomas that he was president of the executive board, and this is what prompted this answer by Mr. Lukic. Although, the issue that he was president was actually never raised by Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And the entire speech that you made now as you stood up a second time you made while the interpreter was talking, so I was hearing two people at the same time, so I missed out on the first part of that statement. Of course I can read what the -- I don't know who was being transcribed, whether you or her. I see it's the interpreter who was being transcribed. What were you saying, Mr. Lukic, when you stood up now the second time?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Thomas mentioned like in the transcript that Mr. Nikolic was in executive board, page 77, and we heard in B/C/S and Mr. Nikolic too that he was the president of executive board. And that's why he made that kind of answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Can we just get that interpretation corrected to the witness so that he can give you an appropriate answer, Mr. Thomas?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I can do that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: General, you asked me the source of these statements that I've been putting to you. The source of these statements is the website for the general and admiral's club of the Republic of Serbia. That is the source.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for this source. Could you please tell me who signed this text?

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: No, I cannot, sir. It appears on your website. But let me ask you this question: Do you agree with the statement that I've read out?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: With which parts do you disagree?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I can't read English, could you please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: Okay. FRY Yugoslavia did something not a single other country has ever done. FRY -- Federal Republic of Yugoslavia extradited to the International Criminal Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia the following persons: Its president, the president of the Republic of Serbia, deputy prime minister of the federal government, minister of defence, two chiefs of the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia, one army commander, and deputy minister of the interior. They were extradited only because they had carried out their duty in a professional manner pursuant to the constitution of a sovereign state, Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and defended their country from terrorism/separatism, and from the NATO aggression.

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this is a combination of a sort. This entire passage is something that no general can ever utter, and I'm not sure, maybe a part of this was taken from an e-mail or something. I was never on a meeting where this was discussed. In the continuation here, it is mentioned that they defended their homeland pursuant to the relevant legislation of their county, and this is why they had to be provided with all the necessary support.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic, the question to you is not whether you were present when those were written or whether you were the author. The question to you is, do you agree with the statement or not? If you agree you say yes, I do agree; if you do not agree, you say I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Prosecutor asked me which parts of this statement I can agree with, and I said, I disagree with the part prior to a full stop, to where -- I'm not sure I can read this correctly. The second part is the part that I do agree with, and I can't agree with the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry, my mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: So, I'm sorry, General. Can I just check the transcript for a moment. So we are clear, you said you agreed with the second part of the statement. That's what the transcript says; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STAMENKO NIKOLIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I think it starts with "they were" and from there on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not want to suggest anything to Mr. Thomas, but Mr. Thomas gave me in Serbian those words that he is now reading, so shouldn't we provide the witness with the Serbian version rather than have him read the transcript in English which he can't understand?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I understand my friend's suggestion, Your Honour. I chose to put the proposition first before using the document if necessary. The general has adopted the proposition and responded to it so I don't feel the need to do that, and, in fact, Your Honours, that at this point concludes my cross-examination. I don't intend to revisit the matter in respect of which General Nikolic was to seek legal advice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You don't -- oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. THOMAS
utterances.text: I don't intend to revisit the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Any re-examination, Mr. Lukic? To finish by quarter to?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I certainly won't be able to finish this today. I can start, and I'm prepared to start with some questions for these seven minutes, or we can allow the witness to have some rest because he will certainly have to be here tomorrow again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. If that's what you wish, that's fine. Mr. Nikolic, Mr. Thomas has just indicated that he is not going to follow-up that subject for which we thought you must get a lawyer. I'm not going to mention it because we are in open session. Okay. So there is no need for you to go and look for legal advice.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I make a proposal myself, as a witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What proposal do you want to make, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask you, if possible, I'm not sure how long this could take because I do have some family issues and I've been here for a long time already, so if it is possible to complete this today, this would be my plea with this court because I have been informed that my wife and child are not well, and I also have some problems concerning the employment of my son. I would like to resolve these problems as soon as possible, so if at all possible, I would kindly ask you to finish this today. Obviously if Your Honours are capable of granting this, I'm able to continue answering any questions today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Unfortunately before I give you the floor, Mr. Lukic. Unfortunately, Mr. Nikolic, there are many cases taking place in the building here, and there are only a few courtrooms, so there is no courtroom available this afternoon for us to carry on with your case. Other cases are going to be sitting. So it is not possible to finish with you today. However, let me just find out from the lawyers whether they may want you to stand down and go and attend to your problems and then come back later or whether they have any other solution that they can propose to come to your rescue. Mr. Lukic, you are on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can inform Your Honours and the witness that I could complete my redirect examination in approximately 40 minutes. Now, I'm not sure whether Your Honours will have any questions for the witness. As far as I know, we were supposed to sit in the afternoon tomorrow, possibly if we are done by 4.00 p.m. tomorrow, the witness might take an evening flight if the witness unit can see to that. So possibly Mr. Nikolic could make his suggestion now and see if this is acceptable to him or not, or if he could come back after the Easter break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Apparently we just need you for under an hour tomorrow, would that be okay, just for an extra day? I know you have been here for a very long time. The alternative is going to be that you go away and then come back for 40 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not accept to appear here again tomorrow. I do not accept the continuation of this proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not even in Serbian could I understand you, General.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with these proceedings being continuing tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Nikolic. We'll certainly finish with you tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Judge Picard is just indicating that tomorrow morning there is a courtroom available if that would help, that means that everybody must be in a position to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no problem with that, sir. And possibly it might be easier for the witness unit to organise the transportation of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: How do the interpreters and everybody else feel about it including the stenographer and all the other technical people?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: I think for the interpretation, Your Honour, there wouldn't be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much for your co-operation. We'll then adjourn to tomorrow morning at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are very welcome, sir. Before I forget, you may not discuss with anybody this case until you are excused tomorrow, okay, especially not your lawyers. Okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never seen him anyway, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
